title: PRP: Pan-Retinal Photocoagulation Mastery
summary: The definitive surgical laser intervention for ischemic retinal diseases, primarily Proliferative Diabetic Retinopathy (PDR). By selectively destroying peripheral photoreceptors, PRP reduces metabolic demand and suppresses the production of Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor (VEGF).

sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Pan-Retinal Photocoagulation (PRP) is a thermal laser procedure applied to the peripheral retina. Its primary goal is to induce the regression of neovascularization (NV) by ablating ischemic retinal tissue, thereby reducing the drive for vasoproliferative factors like VEGF and improving the oxygenation of the remaining viable retina.

sections.title: DRS High-Risk Characteristics (HRCs)
content: NVD > 1/4 to 1/3 disc area
Any NVD associated with Vitreous Hemorrhage (VH) or Preretinal Hemorrhage
NVE > 1/2 disc area associated with Vitreous Hemorrhage
Presence of Neovascularization of the Iris (NVI) or Angle (NVA)

branches: Reduction of Oxygen Consumption: Destroys high-metabolic-rate photoreceptors
Improved Inner Retinal Oxygenation: Allows oxygen from choroid to reach inner retina
Downregulation of Cytokines: Significant drop in intraocular VEGF levels
RPE Stimulation: Production of anti-angiogenic factors (e.g., PEDF)

rows: Higher power needed due to short duration

sections.title: Treatment Anatomy & Zones
content: Step 1: Posterior Border - 2 disc diameters from the foveal center.
Step 2: Nasal Border - 1 disc diameter from the optic disc margin.
Step 3: Superior/Inferior Borders - Beyond the vascular arcades.
Step 4: Peripheral Extent - To the equator or beyond (ora serrata in severe cases).

sections.title: Indications Beyond Diabetes
content: Central Retinal Vein Occlusion (CRVO) - Ischemic type (10 DD non-perfusion)
Hemicentral Retinal Vein Occlusion
Branch Retinal Vein Occlusion (BRVO) with NV
Ocular Ischemic Syndrome (OIS)
Sickle Cell Retinopathy (Stage 3+)
Eales Disease

content.explanation: 3 sessions (if manual), 2 disc diameters from fovea, 1 disc diameter from optic nerve.

sections.title: Immediate Post-Op Complications
content: Choroidal Effusion / Ciliary Body Detachment
Acute Angle Closure (anterior displacement of lens-iris diaphragm)
Exacerbation of Macular Edema (CME)
Transient IOP Spike
Accidental Foveal Burn (Visual Disaster)

rows: Minimal to no leakage (stays within vessel)

sections.title: Surgical Pearl: The 'Filler' Technique
content: Always treat the inferior retina first; if a VH occurs during the session, superior burns are still achievable.
Use a Goldmann 3-mirror or Mainster PRP lens for optimal visualization of the periphery.
Avoid visible retinal vessels to prevent hemorrhage.
Ensure retrobulbar or sub-Tenon's anesthesia if patient is unable to tolerate laser or if long sessions are planned.

sections.title: Modern Advances: DRCR.net Protocol S
sections.content: Protocol S compared PRP vs. Ranibizumab (0.5mg) for PDR. Findings: Anti-VEGF is non-inferior to PRP for visual acuity through 5 years. Anti-VEGF resulted in less peripheral field loss and fewer vitrectomies but requires high patient compliance for repeated injections.

sections.title: Red Flags: When to STOP Laser
content: Tractional Retinal Detachment (TRD) involving or threatening the macula (PRP can worsen traction via 'crunch' syndrome)
Dense Vitreous Hemorrhage obscuring view (requires Vitrectomy/Endo-laser)
Patient Vasovagal Response
Poor pupillary dilation (requires indirect ophthalmoscope laser delivery)

sections.title: Pre-Procedure Diagnostic Workup
content: 1. BCVA and IOP measurement.
2. Dilated Fundus Exam (DFE) with Scleral Depression.
3. Wide-field Fundus Photography.
4. Fluorescein Angiography (FA) to identify areas of NVE and non-perfusion.
5. OCT Macula to check for co-existing DME (determines if Anti-VEGF is needed first).

sections.title: Prognosis & Follow-up
content: Regression of NV typically occurs within 4-6 weeks.
Follow-up: Every 4-8 weeks initially to assess regression.
Supplemental (Fill-in) Laser: Needed in up to 25% of cases with persistent NV.
If NV progresses despite maximal PRP: Consider Anti-VEGF or Pars Plana Vitrectomy (PPV).
